details:
**144,000**
Based on the Book of Revelation, Jehovah's Witnesses believe that exactly 144,000 faithful Christians, the "anointed," will go to heaven to rule with Christ as co-rulers in God's Kingdom. Other faithful believers, the "great crowd" or "other sheep," hope to live forever on a restored paradise Earth.

**Refusal of blood transfusions**
Witnesses refuse transfusions of whole blood and its major components, even in life-threatening situations. They base this on biblical commands to "abstain from blood" (for example, Acts 15), and it is their best-known and most controversial medical stance.

**Charles Taze Russell and the Bible Students**
The movement grew out of the Bible Student movement started by Charles Taze Russell in Pittsburgh in the 1870s. Russell was mocked for promoting "Miracle Wheat," a seed his publications claimed was unusually productive.

**The Watchtower and the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society**
The Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society is the legal and publishing body of the Jehovah's Witnesses. Its flagship magazine, The Watchtower, founded by Russell in 1879, is one of the most widely distributed magazines in the world, and Witnesses hand it out along with Awake!

**New World Translation**
The Witnesses' own translation of the Bible. It renders John 1:1 as "the Word was a god," reflecting their rejection of the Trinity and their view that Jesus is a created being distinct from Jehovah. It also translates the Greek word stauros as "torture stake" rather than "cross," since Witnesses believe Jesus died on an upright pole and do not use the cross as a symbol.

**Kingdom Halls**
The Witnesses' plain meeting places for worship, used instead of churches. They typically have no crosses, icons, or other religious imagery.

**Door-to-door preaching**
Witnesses are famous for proselytizing door to door and for public "cart witnessing" with literature displays. Members consider preaching about God's Kingdom a core religious duty.

**Disfellowshipping**
The Witnesses' form of excommunication for members who commit serious sins without repenting or who reject the group's teachings. Other members, including family, are expected to shun those disfellowshipped, though they may be reinstated if they repent and "come back."

**Joseph Franklin "Judge" Rutherford**
Russell's successor as president of the Watch Tower Society. In 1931 he adopted the name "Jehovah's Witnesses," based on Isaiah 43:10, partly to set his followers apart from other Bible Student groups.

**Governing Body and the "faithful and discreet slave"**
The Governing Body is a small group of elders at the Witnesses' headquarters that directs doctrine and organization. Witnesses identify it with the "faithful and discreet slave" of Matthew 24, which Jesus appoints to provide spiritual "food at the proper time."

**Lord's Evening Meal (Memorial)**
The Witnesses' only annual religious observance, commemorating Jesus's death. It is held on the date corresponding to Nisan 14 of the Hebrew calendar, and only those who believe they are among the anointed 144,000 partake of the bread and wine.

**Rejection of birthdays, holidays, and hellfire**
Witnesses do not celebrate birthdays, Christmas, or Easter, viewing them as having pagan origins. They also reject the doctrines of an immortal soul and eternal torment in hell, teaching that the wicked simply cease to exist.

**1975 prediction**
Under the influence of Fred Franz, a leading theologian who later became the Society's president, Witness publications suggested that Armageddon and Christ's thousand-year reign might begin around 1975. Its failure led many members to leave.

**Photo-Drama of Creation**
An eight-hour 1914 presentation produced under Russell, combining films, slides, and recorded narration (including Russell's own voice) to tell the story of the Bible from creation to the end of the thousand-year reign of Christ.

**Two-witness rule and abuse controversy**
Witness congregations traditionally required two witnesses to an act of wrongdoing (or a confession) before taking judicial action. Critics argue that this policy helped conceal child sexual abuse within the organization.
